name: dune-sentinel-fix-opening-radio-occlusion
title: Keep opening radio messages clear of the aircraft
instruction:
Immediately after starting a sortie, the CORRIDOR CONTROL message covers the lower central flight view and obscures the player aircraft. Keep radio messages readable without covering the aircraft or the immediate firing view, and keep simultaneous flight warnings and radio messages separate. Preserve message text, timing, flight controls and the rest of the flight display.

Enter starts flight from the menu. W accelerates; S brakes; A/D roll; Down pitches up and Up pitches down; Q/E yaw. Tab selects a target and holding F looks toward it. LeftControl fires the cannon and SpaceBar fires a missile. Use short braking inputs to avoid a stall.

Verification deliverable: leave Tests/opening_radio_occlusion_route.json as a JSON list of events {"t": seconds after level start, "key": an Unreal key name, "press": true or false}. Use at most 400 events, all within 118 seconds, include every key release and observation pauses, and begin from a fresh level load. Use keyboard presses only; do not rely on cursor movement, menu clicks, controller input, resolution changes or restarting the application. Start the sortie and leave the chase view steady while the opening radio message is visible, then wait long enough to observe it disappear naturally. No enemy encounter is needed. Validate the route in the running game after the final change and adjust its timing to show the requested result. Keep the existing visual style; do not add debug labels or demonstration-only overlays.

checks.name: change_review
checks.question: Does the radio placement change keep callouts clear of the player view and simultaneous flight warnings without changing their timing or text? Evaluate only the radio presentation change in the reference. Its parked-aircraft camera, terrain sampling, exposure, material, horizon, test-fixture and replay changes are unrelated and not required.

rubric.criterion: Radio messages use a location clear of the lower central aircraft/firing view while retaining readable text and framing.
When a flight warning and radio message coexist, their occupied areas are separate rather than overlapping.
Opening and later radio content, durations and normal expiration remain unchanged.
Existing flight controls, instruments, score and weapons panels continue to work without unrelated gameplay or scene changes.

checks.name: opening_radio_clear
checks.question: In the before/after route plays during the opening nine seconds of flight, is CORRIDOR CONTROL readable above the lower central aircraft view, leaving the aircraft and immediate firing view clear, and does it clear normally afterward? Use the route for the timed callout; reference idle/default-drive frames are context only, with no reference-route assumption.

rubric.criterion: While the opening CORRIDOR CONTROL panel is visible, its opaque rectangle no longer covers the lower-center player aircraft or immediate forward firing view.
The radio heading and opening message remain readable in a distinct upper-central area, without covering the top-center score or bottom-center weapons panel.
After the normal opening-message interval, the radio panel clears while the ordinary flight HUD and sortie continue.

checks.name: worked_well
checks.question: Did the developer work as a careful game developer would on this task: finding what causes the problem or what the change touches, changing only what the task needs, and checking the result in the built, running game?

rubric.criterion: Before changing code or assets it looked at the parts of the game the task concerns (read the relevant code, data or logs, or played the game), rather than editing blindly.
It built the game after its changes and fixed the build errors it caused; its last build succeeded, and the grader's build of where it ended succeeded.
After its last change it ran the game and looked at the outcome the task asks for (screenshots, the log or the player's track), and acted on what it saw.

It changed only what the task needs: no unrelated rewrites, no disabling or deleting features, checks or content to make a problem go away, and no attempt to read the grader, the game's later history or anything outside the project.
